ethiopia.title: Tigray's Unfinished Struggle - From Historical Betrayal to Self-Determination
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Tigray's Unfinished Struggle - From Historical Betrayal to Self-Determination - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Tigray's Unfinished Struggle - From Historical Betrayal to Self-Determination 20 November 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) opinion By Negasi Awetehey Addis Abeba — Tigray's dynamic relationship with the modern Ethiopian state has been shaped by a historical paradox and contradiction: Tigray has been both a target of state oppression, betrayal, and genocide and, at critical moments, an influential participant in shaping the Ethiopian state itself. The Meles Zenawi era brought a long-awaited sense of relief and ecstasy to the people of Tigray after years of struggle, suffering, and uncertainty. This shift from prolonged agony to renewed hope was captured in the title of the late Dr. Solomon Enkuay's book, The Agony and Ecstasy of Tigray --a title that evokes historical contradictions: the enduring pain of oppression and conflict, alongside the exhilaration of hard-won political transformation and a new social contract. Under the EPRDF-led Ethiopian state, the people of Tigray were encouraged to believe in a shared identity founded on self-determination, equality, and mutual respect. Placing uncritical faith in the Ethiopian state, Tigrayans prioritized peace, development, and coexistence, often at the expense of safeguarding Tigray's long-term benefits. Today, that trust has been shattered, leaving behind a profound sense of collective betrayal. The promise of equality, mutual respect, and unity in diversity has become an illusion. Hated throughout history, yet ever-present Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines The land of Tigray has witnessed some of the most frequent and brutal battles in human history. Millennial before the formation of Ethiopia, Tigray endured wars. Before the 2020 war, I used to hear elders saying more than 30 battles had been fought in Tigray. Figures from the center to dehumanize, especially driven by the hate of the 1970s/80s TPLF movement in the north but Tigrayans, manipulate and label it ' ሰሜኑ ሁሌ ጦርነት: የተረገመ ምድር' (the north is always at war: the cursed land). From an archaeological perspective, the earliest destruction dates back to the D'mt period (5th century BC). This was destruction of monumental temples and palaces an era when there was no world order, security and sovereignty, when a powerful empire from afar could invade any group or polity at will. Tigray, even in the age of world order and sovereignty, has endured foreign invasions and wars. Ethiopia's political sovereignty has done little to ensure the security and sovereignty of the Tigray people. Leaving ancient conflicts aside, modern wars in Tigray have put the state acting as either an indifferent or an aggressor or in alliance with the foreign forces. There was also a process that, under the guise of nation-building, the Ethiopian state fractured Tigray's territory and stripped its autonomy and capacity--deliberately leaving it weak and vulnerable to foreign invasion and internal suppression. Because the agency is in the hands of the Ethiopian state, and the same agency adding other foreign agencies has been used to invade Tigray. The 2020-2022 war waged against Tigray by the Prosperity Party-led Ethiopia demonstrates that one hardly needs to study history to witness this ugliest repetition. This government's attempt to decimate Tigray brought Eritrean forces and other drone powers with geopolitical interests. History repeats itself, but each repetition grows uglier. Another unsettling pattern for Tigray is that the broader Ethiopian populace within the country's map is not aware of Ethiopia's sovereignty and the dignity of its people. Instead, they have been manipulated into aligning with foreign forces to annihilate their own fraternal neighbor, Tigray. Meresa Tsehaye, a scholar of political science and security studies, underscores Tigray's dual position as a historically marginalized periphery within the modern Ethiopian state and a strategic part of the wider Horn of Africa. Caught between regional rivalries and competing geopolitical interests, Tigray remains vulnerable to the ambitions of global powers, Middle Eastern actors, and East African states. These overlapping geopolitical, geo-cultural, and geostrategic dynamics risk perpetuating Tigray's role as a hotspot of regional instability, where external interests overshadow its people's rights, security, and aspirations. The recurring cycle of invasion underscores the imperative of a sovereign future for Tigray. The only way to prevent war--the ugliest reality Tigrayans have abhorred throughout history, yet one that remains ever-present--is to secure the future and sovereignty. The Ethiopian government's war on Tigray started in 2020 but has never stopped. The exercise of Tigray's right to self-determination has been pushed aside. Unless this trajectory is reversed, Tigray faces the risk of being erased from the map and its people being wiped out. If this is not possible, political subjugation and assimilation remain the likely scenarios. Reversing this course is imperative for Tigray to safeguard its people, restore their dignity, and secure their right to determine their own future. Existential incompatibility of PP Ideology, Tigray nationalism The relationship between the PP's ideology and Tigrayan identity is fundamentally defined by a profound asymmetry: that between the perpetrator and the victim of betrayal, genocide, and violence. Their relationship is characterized by a fundamental contradiction--one resembling that between the killer and the killed, the perpetrator and the victim, or the betrayer and the betrayed. Although the word "Prosperity" ostensibly evokes progress, growth, and development, it has acquired an altogether different and deeply pejorative meaning in the popular consciousness of Tigray. Through a bitter linguistic play on words, Prosperity (ብልጽግና) has been recast as ብዕልግና (Biligina) in Tigrigna--a term associated with vulgarity, moral corruption, and misconduct. Consequently, Tigrayans who chose to align themselves with or join the PP came to be branded ባዕሊጉ (Baeligu), a charged label that, in this context, conveys profound condemnation of what is perceived as a betrayal of collective values, dignity, and solidarity. The post-Pretoria chapter was supposed to prove if the Prosperity Party had anything to offer Tigray--peace, justice, restoration, or rehabilitation. Instead, Tigray stood amidst ruin: over 600,000 killed, millions displaced , and its essential health, education, and transport infrastructure systematically looted and destroyed. Rather than repairing this damage , the regime has launched a new campaign to finish what it started and conquer the region completely. Ultimately, the ruling party has put nothing on Tigray's table except death or subjugation. The choice before Tigray is not simply between competing political arrangements ..." Across all phases of the war, Tigray's heritage--ancient and modern, sacred and secular--was targeted in a deliberate attempt to break a nation's spirit. From medieval monasteries to modern museums and historic icons, the assault aimed directly at what Tigrayans hold as their living soul. This physical destruction works hand-in-hand with historical abuse: through epistemic erasure, historiographical hegemony, and revisionist appropriation, ruling party figures seek to rewrite the legacy that their ethnic base belongs to the ancient legacy and history in Tigray. It is a dual-pronged strategy of cultural erasure and historical theft--destroying a people's living identity while co-opting their ancient legacy to legitimize the incumbent's party authority. Ultimately, the Prosperity Party's strategy is designed to weaken and depopulate substantive political entities like Tigray, replacing legitimate regional leadership with subservient proxies to entrench OPDO (currently, Oromo Prosperity Party) political and economic dominance. By attempting to project power into strategic maritime corridors like Assab, the ruling apparatus seeks to consolidate indefinite and irreversible rule--a centralized trajectory that is fundamentally incompatible with Tigray's historical identity and current struggle for self-determination. Self-Determination: Earned, learned, and craved Let us consider the words of Ms. Atsede Gebremedhin (a member of Tigray's 'Shig Weyane' (Revolutionary Torch) in the 1980s. She emphasized her message in Tigrigna, essentially conveying that although her generation envisioned Tigray's future within a federal framework, Ethiopian unity must never be traded for subjugation. When the choice is between self-determination and slavery, the pursuit of independence becomes unavoidable. Her words underscore a timeless principle: no political arrangement is worth sacrificing a people's freedom, dignity, and right to determine their own future. She further detailed her position, which can be, excerpted from the full speech, distilled into the following terms: "...regarding separation [from Ethiopia], we choose separation [independence]. Father Kidanu has been saying, 'We have separation as a second option.' We are putting it as an option, but if a progressive government is promulgated in Ethiopia, it [separation] will not be put as an option. It should not be taken that way. Only if a reactionary and slave system is to come to Ethiopia, we will have to separate ourselves to escape the slavery [oppression]. Therefore, separation is from the slavery and not from working-class people of Ethiopia." More than four decades later, Tigray has endured not only prolonged instability but also the devastating crime of genocide. Its longstanding adversaries, having regrouped after their defeat, returned with renewed force to inflict another wave of devastation marked by persecution, torture, genocide, and betrayal. These experiences have brought the question of self-determination back to the forefront of political consciousness. The aspiration for independence has increasingly gained prominence, finding expression through diverse political platforms, organized movements, public discourse, and cultural expression. Music, in particular, has become an important vehicle for expressing Tigrayan identity, historical consciousness, and national aspirations. Songs such as ዓዲ ኣላትኒ (I Have a Country), ሃ ገር እየ ዝደሊ (What I Want Is Independence), ትግራዋነት (The Essence of Being Tigrayan), ትግራይ ዓደይ (Tigray, My Nation), ትግራይ ኵሕሎ (Beautiful Tigray), ት ግራይ ምልባማ (Tigray, the Land of Wisdom), and many others reflect the growing significance of national identity, belonging, and aspirations for a sovereign future. This aspiration is neither new nor detached from history. It is rooted in generations of struggle and shaped by the historical experience of imperial nation-building and its devastating consequences for Tigray. It has been earned through sacrifice, strengthened by historical experience, and sustained by an enduring desire for freedom and a secured future. Yet, alongside this growing sense of national purpose, one fundamental question remains: How can this aspiration be translated into a viable, sustainable, and peaceful political future for Tigray? One step into a cruel destiny For the Prosperity government, war has served--and continues to serve--as an instrument for breaking the will, resistance, and collective determination of the people of Tigray. When the regime deploys starvation, foreign military forces, political coercion, and the co-optation of local elites to subdue an entire population, the struggle for self-determination ceases to be merely a political preference. It becomes an indispensable safeguard against subjugation and the permanent erosion of a people's freedom. A sober assessment of post-Pretoria reveals a deeply unsettling reality: Tigray appears to be entering the opening phase of a cruel political destiny--subjugation under the rule of the Prosperity government. As Tigray remains unliberated and increasingly subjected to the authority of the central regime, Ethiopia's overriding objective appears to be the dismantling of the political and institutional foundations that sustain Tigray's resistance and struggle for self-determination. Under the guise of pacification and political normalization, the federal government, helped by some Tigrayans who made their peace with the prime minister, appears to be pursuing a strategy of neutralizing resistance through the co-optation of Tigray's political and military elites. By offering administrative appointments, financial and material inducements, and assurances of personal survival, it seeks to hollow out the liberation struggle from within. Former defenders of Tigray's political aspirations risk becoming instruments and mouthpieces of the very central authority they once opposed. This political realignment risks a deeper ideological capitulation. A collective consciousness once anchored in freedom, dignity, and self-determination is gradually giving way to enforced subjugation and political assimilation. As former defenders align themselves with the very authority they once opposed, the moral and political foundations of the struggle erode, undermining its unifying force and leaving society increasingly disarmed--both politically and psychologically--and pressured to surrender long-term freedom for the precarious promise of immediate stability and survival. For those aligned with Abiy Ahmed's government, life under external control appears increasingly acceptable and normal. For those who continue to resist, however, subjugation remains unacceptable at any cost. Meanwhile, the central regime and its local partners increasingly portray the historical struggle led by the TPLF as outdated, destructive, or an obstacle to "peace and development." As these narratives take hold, submission risks being recast as political pragmatism, while historical memory and collective political consciousness are distorted or erased. Future generations may consequently be led to view the sacrifices of their predecessors and the TPLF's struggle not as acts of resistance and defense of the right to self-rule but as misguided and costly mistakes. Coercive assimilation, state-led social engineering What is presented as integration may, under occupation and political subordination, become a state-engineered project of assimilation. By extending central government institutions and security structures into Tigray's social and political life, the state could displace local authority, dismantle sovereign institutions, and erode the foundations of self-governance. Prolonged military occupation could thus serve not merely to administer territory but to impose a far-reaching political and social transformation. This process could entail the imposition of political, cultural, and administrative arrangements through military coercion, legislative control, divide-and-rule tactics, and the systematic suppression of local autonomy. Rather than recognize Tigray's distinct historical experience and political aspirations, the central state could seek to remake its institutions and public life in its own image and in accordance with its political priorities. The danger extends beyond institutional control to demographic and territorial engineering. In the aftermath of mass atrocities, such developments raise grave concerns about whether political domination could evolve into a broader project of demographic transformation, threatening the long-term continuity of the Tigray people. As this trajectory becomes entrenched, many Tigrayans--particularly those unwilling to abandon the pursuit of self-determination--may come to see leaving their homeland as the only remaining means of resisting subjugation. Those who remain, meanwhile, could find themselves trapped in a deeply fractured society, divided between accommodation and resistance, privilege and deprivation, and outward compliance and inward resentment. Tigray risks becoming a society of happy slaves and unhappy slaves--one in which subjugation is normalized for some and silently endured by others. This division between those aligned with the central government and those resisting subjugation could harden into an entrenched system of divide and rule. By cultivating competing loyalties and interests within Tigrayan society, the regime could fracture collective solidarity, weaken organized resistance, and obstruct a unified political response. The result could be an "enemy within" syndrome, in which internal suspicion becomes a major obstacle to future unity. Mutual distrust could gradually replace the quiet solidarity, shared understanding, and knowing glances through which Tigrayans sustained one another during the darkest years of siege and blockade. A society once united by shared suffering and resistance could become consumed by suspicion over who has accommodated the system, who has resisted it, and who can still be trusted. Indefinite social discord The existing horizontal divisions within Tigrayan elites--expressed through political realignments, competing strategic visions, and conflicting interpretations of the postwar order--risk hardening into a prolonged and intergenerational rupture. If centralizing and assimilationist policies become entrenched, Tigray could face not only a political struggle over its future but also an internal war over its history, identity, and collective memory. Self-determination must once again become the organizing principle of Tigray's political future." One generation may grow increasingly exposed to central government-sponsored narratives, while another remains committed to preserving Tigray's historical struggle for self-rule rights, convictions, and aspirations. Such a rupture would not remain confined to political organizations or public institutions. It could penetrate the most intimate structures of the society. The long-term damage would extend far beyond political disagreement, undermining the social trust upon which collective life depends. The collapse of social contract of sacrifice Perhaps one of the most devastating long-term consequences of an unaddressed political defeat and perceived internal betrayal would be the destruction of society's capacity for collective mobilization. When the social contract of sacrifice is broken, a profound cynicism may take hold toward political leadership, military institutions, and the very causes for which ordinary people were once prepared to make extraordinary sacrifices. For a population to endure the horrors of war, there must be a fundamental, often unspoken covenant among the people, their fighters, their leadership, and the cause they serve. That covenant rests on a shared understanding: sacrifice must have meaning; those who fall must be remembered and honored; the suffering of the population must not be exploited; and leaders must not trade away the collective cause for their personal security or political survival. When this covenant is violated, the consequences can endure for generations. The public may lose confidence in those who call for sacrifice, and future appeals for mobilization may be met with profound skepticism. People may no longer regard military mobilization as an honorable defense of their homeland and collective aspirations but as a political instrument through which ordinary citizens bear the ultimate costs while political and military elites negotiate their own survival and interests. The memory of betrayal can therefore become a powerful deterrent to future collective action. Even when an existential threat emerges, a population that has lost confidence in its leadership may hesitate to mobilize, fearing that its sacrifices will once again be squandered or betrayed. The f
ethiopia.summary: Tigray's complex relationship with Ethiopia is marked by historical oppression and betrayal, juxtaposed with moments of significant political influence. The era of Meles Zenawi initially brought hope to Tigrayans, who believed in a shared identity based on self-determination and equality. However, this trust has been shattered, revealing a deep sense of betrayal as the Ethiopian state has failed to protect Tigray's autonomy and rights. The 2020-2022 war exemplified this betrayal, leading to immense loss of life and destruction of infrastructure. The Prosperity Party's ideology has further marginalized Tigray, fostering resentment and a desire for self-determination among its people. Cultural erasure and historical appropriation have compounded these grievances, as Tigrayans seek to reclaim their identity and future. Amidst ongoing violence and geopolitical manipulation, the aspiration for independence has gained momentum, reflecting a historical struggle for dignity and sovereignty. The question remains: how can Tigray's aspirations for self-determination translate into a sustainable political future? (159 words)

somalia.content: GCC backs UAE, rejects Somalia’s allegations of interference - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME POLITICS GCC backs UAE, rejects Somalia’s allegations of interference Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Saturday November 21, 2026 Mogadishu (HOL) — The Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) has condemned statements by Somali government officials accusing the United Arab Emirates of interfering in Somalia's internal affairs, describing the allegations as irresponsible and rejecting what it called misleading media campaigns targeting the Gulf state. In a statement issued Thursday, Nov. 19, GCC Secretary-General Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi expressed support for the UAE amid escalating diplomatic tensions between Mogadishu and Abu Dhabi. advertisements Albudaiwi criticized statements by officials of Somalia's federal government, accusing them of spreading allegations that undermine the UAE's regional and international role. The GCC statement described the remarks as irresponsible and denounced what it called malicious media campaigns directed against one of its member states. The secretary-general defended the UAE's diplomatic activities, saying the country had made significant contributions to regional security, stability and international dialogue. “The UAE’s recent hosting of Russian-Ukrainian talks demonstrates its commitment to regional and international peace and security. These unacceptable allegations seek to undermine our efforts to promote dialogue and cooperation,” he said. Albudaiwi said the allegations against the UAE risked undermining its efforts to promote regional and international cooperation. He emphasized that GCC member states remained committed to advancing peace, stability and prosperity and would reject campaigns intended to damage the reputation of any member state. “The GCC states remain steadfast in their approach to consolidating security, stability, and prosperity, and categorically reject any media campaigns aimed at offending any of their member states. Such campaigns will not affect the continuation of their role in supporting peace and security across the region and the world,” the statement added. The statement comes amid a sharp deterioration in diplomatic relations between Somalia and the UAE following accusations by President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud that Abu Dhabi has interfered in Somalia's domestic political and security affairs. In a televised address Tuesday, Hassan Sheikh accused the UAE of providing political, financial and security support to regional administrations and armed groups operating outside the federal government's control. He also criticized Emirati agreements involving the ports of Berbera, Bosaso and Kismayo, arguing that such arrangements undermine Somalia's sovereignty and should be negotiated through Mogadishu. On Thursday, Somalia's Cabinet ordered the UAE ambassador to leave the country within 72 hours and recalled its ambassador from Abu Dhabi for consultations. The Somali government said the measures were intended to protect its sovereignty, territorial integrity and national unity. The UAE Foreign Ministry responded by condemning what it described as the Somali government's hostile approach, accusing Mogadishu of allowing internal political disputes to damage bilateral relations. Abu Dhabi also said it had closed its embassy in Mogadishu and withdrawn its diplomatic personnel in January 2026, following earlier disagreements over Somalia's cancellation of bilateral agreements. The GCC's latest statement adds a regional dimension to the dispute, with the six-member Gulf bloc publicly defending the UAE against Somalia's accusations. The GCC comprises the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain and Oman. The council did not announce any diplomatic or economic measures against Somalia, limiting its response to a public condemnation of the Somali government's statements and expressions of support for the UAE. somalia.title: Somalia Is Not for Sale — A United People Stand Behind Their Government in Defence of National Sovereignty - Hiiraan Online
somalia.content: Somalia Is Not for Sale — A United People Stand Behind Their Government in Defence of National Sovereignty - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME OPINION Somalia Is Not for Sale — A United People Stand Behind Their Government in Defence of National Sovereignty Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ By Ridwan Yusuf Mohamud Founder and Editor in Chief of Somali Magazine Saturday November 21, 2026 There are moments in a nation’s history when its people must look beyond political differences, regional affiliations and clan divisions to defend something greater than themselves: their country’s sovereignty, independence and national dignity. Somalia is facing such a moment. As diplomatic tensions between Somalia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) intensify, the position taken by the Federal Government has placed an important national question at the centre of public debate: who has the right to determine Somalia’s future? The answer should be clear. It is the Somali people, through their legitimate national institutions and constitutional processes. The Federal Government’s decision to take diplomatic action against the UAE reflects the seriousness of the disagreement over Somalia’s sovereignty and internal affairs. This is not merely a disagreement between two governments. It touches on the fundamental principles of national independence, territorial integrity and the authority of the Somali state. This Is Bigger Than Politics For decades, Somalia has paid a heavy price for internal divisions, political rivalries and external involvement in its affairs. The consequences have been felt by generations of Somalis, from Mogadishu to the regions and across the diaspora. Today, the country cannot afford to allow political disagreements to undermine its national interests. Somalis have every right to disagree with their government, question its decisions and demand accountability. That is part of responsible citizenship. However, when the country’s sovereignty and territorial integrity are at stake, national interests must take precedence over political differences. Standing behind the government’s defence of national sovereignty does not mean giving political leaders a blank cheque. It means recognising that the independence of the Somali state must be protected regardless of who occupies the presidential office. Foreign Partnerships Must Respect Somalia Somalia welcomes international investment, trade, development assistance and security cooperation. The UAE, like other international partners, can play a role in Somalia’s economic development. However, cooperation must be based on mutual respect and recognition of Somalia’s national institutions. No foreign government should be in a position to determine Somalia’s political direction or undermine its territorial integrity. Strategic agreements and security arrangements affecting the country must respect its constitutional framework and national authority. Diplomatic disagreements should be addressed through dialogue, international law and peaceful engagement, but sovereignty must remain the guiding principle. Somalia should never have to compromise its national independence in exchange for investment, financial assistance or diplomatic relationships. Genuine partnerships strengthen nations; they do not weaken their institutions or challenge their territorial integrity. A Message to the Somali People This is a moment for Somalis everywhere to reflect on the kind of country they want to build. A country that speaks with dignity internationally, protects its national interests, strengthens its institutions and makes decisions independently. Political leaders must also recognise that national unity requires responsibility, transparency and inclusive leadership. The government has a duty to protect the country, but it must equally earn public confidence through accountable governance. The Somali people should not allow their differences to become opportunities for external interests to influence the country’s future. From Mogadishu to Hargeisa, Garowe, Kismayo, Baidoa and the Somali diaspora, the principle of national sovereignty deserves serious consideration and collective commitment. The current diplomatic situation should also remind Somali political leaders that the country’s national interests must never become secondary to personal ambitions, regional rivalries or political calculations. Somalia needs a united national position, strong institutions and leadership capable of representing the entire country. Somalia Must Come First The strength of a nation is not measured only by its military capabilities, economic resources or diplomatic relationships. It is also measured by the willingness of its people to defend their independence and stand together when their national interests are challenged. Somalia has endured too much to allow another generation to inherit a divided country. This is not about hostility towards the Emirati people. It is about respect between nations and the fundamental right of Somalia to govern its own affairs. The UAE and Somalia may have a history of economic, diplomatic and security cooperation, but no relationship should come at the expense of Somalia’s sovereignty. Friendship between nations must be built on equality, mutual respect and respect for national institutions. The Somali people must understand that defending their country is not the responsibility of the president alone, nor is it the responsibility of one political party, one region or one community. It is a collective national responsibility. The Somali people may disagree on politics, leadership and government policies, but they should never disagree on the fundamental right of their country to exist as a sovereign and independent nation. This is the time to put Somalia first. To stand above clan divisions, political rivalries and regional differences. To defend the country’s independence while demanding accountable leadership and responsible governance. Somalia belongs to its people. Its sovereignty is not for sale, its territorial integrity is not negotiable, and its future must be determined by Somalis themselves. One nation. One sovereignty. One future. [Photo: Private collection and Johan Nilsson/TT News Agency.] STOCKHOLM, Sweden (Garowe Online) – Sweden's Equality Ombudsman (DO) has taken the Swedish Police to court, accusing them of discriminating against the family of Mohamed, a 14-year-old Somali boy who was killed in July 2023. The case will be heard on May 13, 14 and 27, 2027, after settlement talks failed. Stockholm District Court will decide whether Mohamed's mother and sister were discriminated against because of their ethnic origin, and whether they should receive 300,000 Swedish kronor in compensation. Mohamed lived in the town of Nässjö. In July 2023 he went missing from a children's care facility. His family told police he was in danger, but four days later his body was found near Nynäshamn, south of Stockholm. An investigation by Sveriges Radio found that police did not act while members of the Foxtrot organized crime network abducted and tortured Mohamed. Three men were later sentenced to life in prison for his murder. His friend Layth, also 14, was killed as well. The DO said police did not give Mohamed's mother an interpreter, even though she does not speak Swedish. It also said they failed to contact her again as they had promised. His 12-year-old sister was the one who first spoke to police. In 2025, the Swedish Police admitted they had violated administrative law and the Convention on the Rights of the Child, but they denied discrimination. The lawsuit was filed on January 28, 2026. It is the first discrimination case the DO has brought against the Swedish Police. The case also reached the Swedish Parliament, where lawmakers questioned Justice Minister Gunnar Strömmer about it. Mohamed's family is now waiting for the court's ruling. The case has raised questions about how Swedish police treat families from immigrant communities. In a formal statement issued on November 15 and updated on November 17, the monitoring group stated that Somaliland authorities carried out the executions following presidential authorization without releasing full trial judgments, evidentiary findings, or appeal records for any of the nine men. According to information received by the organization, Ahmed’s immediate family was also not notified prior to his execution. Contradictions in Official Erigavo Records According to SHRMG, Ahmed was participating in a government-ordered security deployment in Erigavo, the regional capital of Sanaag, in May 2024 when an 18-year-old resident, Ayaanle Maxamuud Cumar, was fatally shot. The organization reported that Ahmed had no prior personal relationship with the deceased and caused the death accidentally while acting under official instructions. To substantiate concerns over institutional accountability, the group published three official government letters spanning 2024 and 2025 concerning Cumar’s death. The first letter, issued by the Somaliland Police Force on May 28, 2024, under reference KT/TCB/3/3-24/2024, recorded that Sanaag regional police fatally shot Cumar on May 16, 2024, during security preparations for the May 18 commemorations, and formally requested state compensation for his family. Subsequent ministerial correspondence reinforced that account. On June 29, 2024, then-Interior Minister Mohamed Kaahin Ahmed forwarded the police compensation request to the presidency under reference WAG/XW/412/831/482/06/2024, recommending state payment because the fatality occurred during a government security operation. On April 15, 2025, Minister of Interior and Security Cabdalle Maxamed Carab reiterated the recommendation to the president under reference WAG/AM/XW/121/18/2025. SHRMG noted that while the leaked letters do not independently establish whether compensation was paid or clarify the exact forensic link between the Sanaag regional police account and Ahmed’s prosecution, they demonstrate that authorities formally recognized the shooting as an operational incident warranting state restitution long before executing Ahmed. International Legal Standards and Qisas Claims The rights group argued that executing a defendant for an unintentional or negligent killing during a state mission violates Article 6 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), alongside UN Human Rights Committee General Comment No. 36, which restricts capital punishment strictly to crimes involving intentional killing. The statement also cited fair-trial guarantees under Article 14 of the ICCPR and the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights. While Somaliland authorities have reportedly justified the November 11 executions under the Islamic legal principle of Qisas, SHRMG maintained that invoking religious jurisprudence does not absolve judicial institutions from proving criminal intent, ensuring transparent trials, or verifying whether victims’ families were freely offered the option of blood compensation, known as diya, without coercion. The monitoring group issued ten demands to Hargeisa, calling for the immediate publication of Ahmed’s complete court file, disclosure of operational orders from the May 2024 Erigavo deployment, an independent inquiry into all nine executions, and an immediate moratorium on capital punishment. It also appealed to foreign embassies, UN Special Rapporteurs, and the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights to scrutinize the cases. Broader Scrutiny of Capital Punishment The November 11 deaths marked the second round of executions under President Cirro , following earlier firing-squad executions carried out at Mandera prison in previous years, as FTL Somalia previously reported . Meanwhile, security governance in the wider Sanaag region remains volatile amid overlapping territorial claims and unresolved local disputes, conditions highlighted during recent deadly Sanaag clan conflicts . The Mandera firing-squad executions also took place just days before Mogadishu voted in favor of a global suspension of capital punishment at the United Nations, a diplomatic move examined when Somalia backed a UN moratorium on executions despite continuing to impose death sentences domestically. Barely 48 hours after that New York vote, federal military courts underscored the domestic reliance on capital punishment when Somalia sentenced a NISA soldier to death for murder. FTL Critical Note The documentary record compiled by SHRMG exposes troubling opacity inside Somaliland’s judicial and security apparatus. When police command and two successive interior ministers formally document a fatal shooting as a state-directed security operation warranting government compensation, yet authorities subsequently execute an operative without releasing court judgments or notifying his family, public confidence in due process erodes. This lack of institutional transparency sits uneasily alongside Hargeisa’s sustained diplomatic campaign to present itself to Western capitals and international partners as a stable, rights-respecting democracy worthy of formal statehood recognition. Shielding military and criminal proceedings behind official silence while carrying out irreversible punishments undermines both domestic accountability and Somaliland’s broader claims to rule-of-law governance. somalia.content: Somalia, EU host security talks in Brussels ahead of AUSSOM mandate decision - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME NEWS Somalia, EU host security talks in Brussels ahead of AUSSOM mandate decision Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Saturday November 21, 2026 Mogadishu (HOL) — Somalia and the European Union have jointly hosted a high-level security meeting in Brussels, bringing together representatives from 50 countries and international organizations to discuss Somalia's plan to assume full responsibility for national security as the future of the African Union peacekeeping mission comes under review. The meeting, held Thursday, Nov. 19, focused on Somalia's security transition roadmap, the future of international military assistance and efforts to strengthen the country's security institutions ahead of a United Nations Security Council decision on the mandate of the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM) in December. advertisements According to Somalia's Ministry of Defence, the gathering provided an opportunity for the federal government to present its vision for taking full responsibility for national security while coordinating future support from international partners. Somali Defence Minister Ahmed Moallim Fiqi addressed the opening session, outlining the country's security situation, progress in the transition process and the government's plans to assume greater security responsibilities. Fiqi emphasized the importance of continued international assistance to ensure an orderly transition that reflects Somalia's security priorities and operational needs. Jihan Abdullahi Hassan, senior adviser to President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud on defense affairs, presented Somalia's security transition strategy, outlining the government's proposed framework for transferring responsibilities from international forces to Somali institutions. The meeting was co-chaired by Abdihakim Mohamed Yusuf, chief of staff to the Somali president, and Olof Skoog, deputy secretary-general for political affairs at the European External Action Service. Other participants included Annette Weber, the EU special representative for the Horn of Africa; El Hadji Ibrahima Diene, the African Union special representative for Somalia and head of AUSSOM; and Graham Maitland, the United Nations director for East Africa in the Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs. Representatives from AUSSOM troop-contributing countries, including Djibouti, Ethiopia, Kenya and Uganda, attended the discussions alongside officials from the United States, United Kingdom, Türkiye, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait and EU member states. According to the European Union, participants discussed future international engagement in Somalia's security framework and the importance of maintaining close coordination during the transition. They agreed to continue technical and political consultations to develop a common understanding of the next steps. The EU also emphasized that a sustainable security framework would require broader political agreement among Somali stakeholders, highlighting the importance of an inclusive political settlement. The discussions come as AUSSOM faces uncertainty over its future financing and operations. The mission's current United Nations authorization expires Dec. 31, 2026, and the Security Council is expected to consider its renewal next month. Funding shortages have raised concerns about the ability of African Union forces to maintain operations and continue supporting Somali troops fighting al-Shabab. Some troop-contributing countries have also announced plans to reduce or withdraw their military presence, increasing pressure on Somalia to strengthen its armed forces and assume responsibility for areas previously secured by international peacekeepers. AUSSOM, which replaced the African Union Transition Mission in Somalia in January 2025, supports Somali security forces in operations against al-Shabab and in protecting strategic locations. Despite years of military operations, al-Shabab continues to carry out attacks and maintain a presence in parts of southern and central Somalia. The European Union reaffirmed its commitment to supporting Somalia's peace, stability and security, including a transition led and managed by Somali institutions. Officials attending the Brussels meeting welcomed Somalia's proposed security transition framework and called for closer cooperation to ensure that progress is sustained. However, no final agreement on future security arrangements or new financial commitments was announced. Dated November 20, the decree ratifies the “Agreement on In-Kind Donation Support Between the Government of the Republic of Türkiye and the Government of the Federal Republic of Somalia,” originally signed in Ankara on July 6, 2022, by Turkish Minister of Environment, Urbanisation and Climate Change Murat Kurum and Somalia’s then-Acting Foreign Minister Balal Mohamed Cusman. The Turkish Parliament previously approved the pact through Law No. 7580 on May 7, 2026. Original MoU / Translated MoU in English . Terms of the Donation and Legal Restrictions Under the agreement, Türkiye will design, construct, and donate embassy premises of up to 3,000 square meters on a 4,918 square meter plot in Ankara’s Gölbaşı district, located at Kızılcaşar quarter, plot number 121186/1. Property rights to the land were transferred to Somalia under a bilateral diplomatic land-swap protocol signed in Istanbul on March 22, 2019. Implementation is tied directly to Türkiye’s national legislation and annual budget allocations. Ankara will select the architectural and engineering contractors under Turkish public procurement laws, determine and allocate all project costs, and supervise construction. If local Turkish zoning or construction regulations change during execution, Türkiye is authorized to reflect those modifications in the building footprint. Ownership of the buildings will transfer to Somalia upon completion and issuance of an occupancy permit, and Mogadishu must commence diplomatic operations inside the compound within three months of handover. Under Article 3, Somalia is committed to using the premises exclusively for embassy functions under the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations. If Somalia terminates its embassy mission in Ankara, ownership automatically reverts to Türkiye. Should the mission relocate elsewhere in the Turkish capital, Somalia cannot sell, lease, exchange, or transfer rights to the property to any third party without Türkiye’s prior written consent. Under Article 5 of the pact, both governments also waived access to external legal remedies, stipulating that any dispute over interpreting or implementing the agreement must be resolved solely through bilateral negotiations without recourse to national courts, international tribunals, or third-party arbitration. The text further specifies that while signed in equally authentic Turkish and English versions, the English version prevails in the event of interpretive divergence. Entry into Force Pending Diplomatic Notification The presidential decision alone does not bring the agreement into force. Under Article 7, the accord takes effect upon receipt of the final written notification through diplomatic channels confirming that both sides have completed their internal legal procedures. The Somali Embassy in Ankara said in a statement on social media that Erdoğan’s approval cleared the construction budget and indicated that building work is expected to begin soon. The ratification arrives more than four years after the initial signing, unfolding against an expansive Turkish security footprint in the Horn of Africa. Türkiye operates its largest overseas military training base in Mogadishu, has trained thousands of Somali soldiers alongside the Haramcad special police unit, as FTL Somalia reported , and has deployed F-16 fighter jets and naval frigates to Somalia, according to FTL Somalia’s coverage . Reciprocal Diplomatic Arrangement The Ankara construction project forms part of a reciprocal diplomatic land arrangement under which Somalia granted Türkiye a coastal plot exceeding 61,000 square meters in Mogadishu, taking part of Lido Beach, where Ankara built its largest embassy complex worldwide. During Turkish parliamentary debates in May 2026, opposition lawmakers questioned the asymmetric terms of the deal, noting that Türkiye is financing both design and construction in Ankara while Somalia contributed only land it had originally received from Türkiye under the 2019 Istanbul protocol. Beyond diplomatic real estate, bilateral engagement has rapidly expanded into strategic sectors. A Turkish delegation including the Turkish Space Agency and defense manufacturer Roketsan visited Mogadishu and Warsheikh this year as cooperation widened into aerospace and advanced defense technology, as FTL Somalia reported , alongside the deployment of Turkish research and fishing vessels to Somali waters, according to FTL Somalia’s coverage . FTL Critical Note While the approval of the Ankara embassy grant resolves a four-year bureaucratic delay and secures a permanent diplomatic facility for Mogadishu, the contract’s legal architecture underscores profound structural asymmetry and risks of diplomatic capture. Under the ratified text, Türkiye designs, procures, funds, and supervises the construction of Somalia’s sovereign mission, retains strict reversionary rights and veto power over any future property transfer, and binds Mogadishu to a dispute-settlement clause barring any appeal to international courts or third-party arbiters. Allowing a host government to design and construct an embassy compound from the ground up also introduces standard counterintelligence and operational security vulnerabilities that sovereign states routinely seek to avoid. More broadly, this diplomatic dependency mirrors a wider pattern in which Somalia’s core state functions, from military command and airspace protection to port operations, state-backed banking , and offshore resource exploration, are increasingly underwritten or managed by Ankara. When a single foreign power constructs a nation’s diplomatic missions abroad while simultaneously maintaining military bases, building a 350 million dollar spaceport in Warsheikh , and guarding offshore oil exploration at home, the boundary between bilateral partnership and entrenched clientelism blurs. This imbalance carries tangible sovereignty costs. As previous federal oversight reviews have demonstrated, domestic watchdogs have struggled to enforce financial transparency on Turkish commercial concessions, with the Auditor General unable to verify 34 million dollars in concession fees from Mogadishu’s port and airport. Heavy reliance on Turkish patronage risks constraining Mogadishu’s independent foreign policy maneuverability, leaving Somali institutions reluctant to scrutinize unfavorable commercial terms or assert regulatory authority when bilateral interests diverge. football.content: أزمة الدوري السوداني.. المريخ يتسلم الحيثيات ويستعد لـ"كاس" أزمة الدوري السوداني.. المريخ يتسلم الحيثيات ويستعد لـ"كاس" مباريات اليوم رياضات كرة القدم الأخبار فيديو البطولات البرامج دول أزمة الدوري السوداني.. المريخ يتسلم الحيثيات ويستعد لـ"كاس" من مباراة سابقة بين عملاقي الكرة السودانية المريخ والهلال (winwin) 20 نوفمبر 2026 أزمة الدوري السوداني.. المريخ يتسلم الحيثيات ويستعد لـ"كاس" الهلال السوداني المريخ الدوري السوداني الممتاز كرة قدم حافظ محمد أحمد الخرطوم winwin أضفنا الى 'غوغل' تسلّم نادي المريخ السوداني، اليوم الجمعة 20 نوفمبر/ تشرين الثاني، الحيثيات التي استندت إليها لجنة الاستئنافات باتحاد كرة القدم السوداني في قرارها القاضي بالتراجع عن حكمها السابق، وتجريد الفريق من لقب النسخة الماضية للدوري الممتاز. وعكفت اللجنة القانونية بالنادي على دراسة هذه الحيثيات التي أعادت اللقب إلى نادي الهلال ، بعد أن كانت اللجنة قد قبلت في وقت سابق طعن المريخ وقررت منحه اللقب، وهو ما أثار ردود أفعال واسعة. المريخ يستعد لجولة جديدة بمحكمة التحكيم الرياضي وتستعد إدارة النادي من خلال فريقها القانوني لإعداد مذكرة وافية لرفعها إلى محكمة التحكيم الرياضية "كاس" خلال الفترة القليلة القادمة، عقب الانتهاء من تقييم حيثيات قرار لجنة الاستئنافات. وتأتي هذه الخطوة استمرارًا لضغط إدارة الرئيس مجاهد سهل على اتحاد كرة القدم ، وتشديد الخناق عليه في حالة كسبه للقضية عبر محكمة التحكيم الرياضي. اقرأ أيضًا مدرب الهلال السوداني يترقب 3 تحديات شاقة في مواجهة الشرطة! الهلال السوداني يتلقى دعما مزدوجا وزينباور يضع حدا للشائعات وتسعى إدارة المريخ لاستعادة لقب الدوري عبر محكمة التحكيم الرياضية "كاس"، في محاولة لتكرار سيناريو عام 2017؛ حين شهدت الكرة السودانية سابقة تاريخية بتتويج الفريق بقرار قضائي إثر شكوى أثارت جدلًا واسعًا، وانتهت بتجريد الغريم التقليدي الهلال من لقب كان قد أحرزه ميدانيًا، ليُمنح للمريخ في خطوة اعتبرت درسًا في الدفاع عن الحقوق عبر المسارات القانونية الدولية. يُذكر أنّ صراعًا قانونيًا محتدمًا نشب بين قطبي الكرة السودانية، عقب طعن المريخ في قانونية مشاركة عدد من محترفي الهلال في مباراة الديربي التي جمعت الفريقين في ختام الموسم. ورغم أنّ لجنة الاستئنافات حسمت القضية لصالح المريخ أولًا، عادت وقبلت طلب الفحص الذي قدمه الهلال لتعيد اللقب إليه مجددًا، مما دفع إدارة المريخ للتصعيد واللجوء إلى محكمة التحكيم الرياضية. النشرة البريدية اشترك معنا بالنشرة البريدية لتصلك آخر أخبار الرياضة اشترك معنا دول كرة القدم الأخبار الدوريات الفرق رياضات التنس كرة السلة رياضات ميكانيكية مبارايات اليوم الأخبار البرامج الفيديو عن الموقع تواصل معنا أعلن معنا وظائف سياسة الخصوصية الشروط والأحكام الملكية الفكرية خريطة الموقع winwin© جميع الحقوق محفوظة 2026 الشروط والأحكام | سياسة الخصوصية مباريات اليوم
football.summary: تسلم نادي المريخ السوداني، في 20 نوفمبر 2026، الحيثيات التي استندت إليها لجنة الاستئنافات باتحاد كرة القدم السوداني في قرارها بإعادة لقب الدوري الممتاز لنادي الهلال، بعد أن كان قد مُنح سابقًا للمريخ. وقد أثار هذا القرار ردود أفعال واسعة، حيث كانت اللجنة قد قبلت في البداية طعن المريخ. الآن، يستعد المريخ لتقديم مذكرة إلى محكمة التحكيم الرياضية "كاس" بعد تقييم الحيثيات، في خطوة تهدف لاستعادة اللقب. يأتي ذلك في إطار الضغط المستمر من إدارة النادي على اتحاد كرة القدم، مستندة إلى تجربة سابقة في 2017 حيث تم منح المريخ اللقب عبر قرار قضائي. الصراع القانوني بين المريخ والهلال يتصاعد، خاصة بعد الطعن في قانونية مشاركة بعض لاعبي الهلال في مباراة الديربي.
